what_it_does: Diffusion models generate images by iteratively removing noise from a picture across many steps, and each step requires running a large neural network. This makes them slow and memory-hungry on dedicated accelerator chips. A common speedup is to use compressed number representations (fewer bits per number) for most of the network while keeping a small number of sensitive values at full precision — a technique called mixed-precision quantization (rounding numbers to use less storage). One particular approach stores only the difference between consecutive steps (differential quantization) to save memory, but it still has to load the original full-precision values from memory to blend with those differences, creating a memory bandwidth bottleneck. MHDiff identifies which pixels are most important (called focal pixels) at the first processing layer and then applies that same set of important pixels throughout all layers, so those pixels always get full-precision treatment while the rest are stored in compact form. A hardware packing module then merges the low-precision and high-precision values into a uniform representation that the chip's processing units can handle efficiently without special-case memory traffic.
